transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lina Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Polaris Product), Arjun Rao (Polaris SRE), Tess Morgan (Privacy), Luke Park (FE)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick agenda: quick hosted API walkthrough, show streaming behaviors and the common params, then talk retries and a small demo from the Console. keep it interactive, stop me anytime.
[00:22] Maya: sounds good, we're especially interested in how streaming impacts latency for our chat widget and how to avoid double messages when a retry happens.
[00:30] Lina: great, we'll show the stream model behavior and then the recommended retry playbook — we've seen customers trip over idempotency on streaming calls.
[01:10] Samir: first, high level. Redwood Hosted offers a /generations or /chat endpoint, streaming as chunked responses so you get tokens as they're generated. it's efficient for UX because you render partial tokens. caveat: streaming doesn't guarantee single delivery on client disconnect + retry unless you manage idempotency tokens.
[01:45] Arjun: can you expand on idempotency? like if our client drops and hits retry, will the model repeat text?
[01:53] Lina: good q. short version: streaming is usually at-least-once for delivered chunks. recommended pattern — use an idempotency key for the generation request and keep a server-side write-ahead log so you can detect duplicate completions. if you can't persist keys, do client-side dedupe comparing leading tokens.
[02:30] Luke: does Redwood reconstitute a stream mid-response if we reattach? like resume?
[02:36] Samir: we don't currently support stream resume out-of-the-box. for that flow many customers append a cursor and request continuation with the partial output as context to avoid re-gen. that costs extra tokens though.
[03:10] Maya: ok. show us the params we should tune for quality vs latency.
[03:20] Lina: sure — the main knobs are temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, and presence/penalty if you use policy models. temperature controls randomness — 0.0 is deterministic, 0.6 is moderate. top_p is nucleus sampling; you can combine them but usually tune one. max_tokens caps generated length — important for cost/latency. also streaming chunk size can be tuned on the client — smaller chunks = earlier UI updates but more overhead.
[04:05] Samir: important practical tip: if you care about latency percentiles, limit max_tokens and also enable prefix caching for repeated prompts e.g., system + few-shot. Redwood Optimize will recommend caching keys and quantization profiles.
[04:40] Arjun: any defaults you recommend for a chat widget with short responses (~40-80 tokens)?
[04:46] Lina: try temperature 0.2-0.4, top_p 0.8-0.95, max_tokens 80-120, stop at newline-based stop sequences. for latency prioritize lower temperature and stricter max_tokens.
[05:30] Samir: now the retry playbook. most common errors you will see: transient 5xx, connection resets, rate limit 429. recommended backoff: exponential backoff with full jitter, start with 200ms base, max backoff 8-10s, and cap retries 3 for interactive UI where duplication is visible. for non-interactive batch jobs you can bump retries and use idempotency for at-most-once semantics.
[06:05] Tess: concerned about duplication leaking PHI — if a generation repeats partially that could be an issue. how do we ensure we don't resend protected transcripts?
[06:15] Lina: you'll need to treat outputs like PII — redact or encrypt in transit and at rest. Redwood supports KMS for customer keys and audit logs per request in the console. also consider server-side dedupe and retention policies; we can disable retention in Private deployments.
[06:55] Samir: demo time. I'll share my screen and walk through the Console quickstart and the trace view.
[07:12] 
[screen share begins — rough notes recorded]
[07:15] Samir: here in the Console you can run a live generation. I'll use the 'chat' quickstart. note the token cost panel on the right — it shows prompt vs generation tokens and estimated $ cost. that's handy for rapid tuning.
[07:40] Lina: also notice the trace ID header — that maps to our request traces and you can export the full latency waterfall for each token. when we run perf tests we look at tail latency (p95/p99) since UX hits those.
[08:05] Luke: is there a programmatic mapping to that trace id? we want to correlate to our logs.
[08:11] Samir: yes — we surface a trace_id response header and you can include our request_id as well. store it with your client logs and you'll have end-to-end traceability.
[08:35] Samir: demo of streaming: I'll choose a 60-token prompt and enable streaming. you should see partial tokens appear in the UI as the model generates.
[08:48] [08:48] Generation stream: "Hello — thanks for reaching out..." (partial chunks)
[09:05] Lina: you may notice intermittent chunk boundaries in the transcript — that's normal depending on model batch scheduling. if you want more frequent chunks, set smaller chunk windows but be mindful of overhead.
[09:30] Arjun: what about retries in streaming specifically — if the connection cuts at token 37, what's the safest flow?
[09:36] Lina: flow A: server receives partial tokens and persist them; client reconnects and requests the remainder using an idempotency key. flow B: client treats any reconnect as a fresh request and uses dedupe on final outputs comparing initial tokens. recommended: server-side persisted idempotency for sensitive apps.
[10:05] Samir: also we recommend including a client-generated request_id header plus a resume_token when you can. resume token is just the last N tokens hash so the server can detect overlap. this is more of an engineering pattern right now than a built-in feature.
[10:40] Maya: can you show what errors look like in the Console traces?
[10:44] Samir: sure — here's a 429 replay I triggered by hammering the endpoint. trace shows backlog on the serving runtime then a 429. the best practice is to implement a queued retry with exponential backoff and respect Retry-After header when present. also implement token bucket client-side rate limiting to smooth spikes.
[11:20] Lina: quick note on types of retries: idempotent-safe retry — safe to retry without duplication (usually for non-streaming with idempotency). best-effort retry — short retry window with UI guardrails. and no-retry for operations that would cause side-effects downstream.
[12:00] Luke: how do we pick between hosted and dedicated? we may start hosted but our volume could justify dedicated in 6-12 months.
[12:08] Samir: typical pattern: start hosted to iterate quickly; if you need strict capacity, isolation, or special network/VPC constraints, move to Dedicated. we can give estimated break-even based on your throughput and token counts — Lina will run a ballpark after the perf test.
[12:35] Arjun: any limits around concurrent streaming sessions per key?
[12:40] Lina: we enforce quotas; hosted tiers have soft limits that can be increased. we advise using backpressure + client circuit breaker and queueing. for Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools so you hit more predictable concurrency.
[13:05] Maya: show us the sample retry snippet for a browser client.
[13:10] Samir: reading from notes: browser flow — don't do expensive retries directly from the browser. instead have your backend own retries and idempotency, return a final message status to the client. sample pseudocode: 1) generate request_id, persist request record with status: pending; 2) call Redwood with idempotency key=request_id; 3) on success mark persisted; 4) if transient failure retry with exponential backoff up to 3 times; 5) if still failing surface friendly UI message ("still generating, retrying in background"). I'll paste this snippet after the call.
[14:00] [14:00] Transcription note: occasional stutters and misrecognized acronyms (SAM L -> SAML).
[14:10] Tess: on compliance: can you walk through retention and encryption options?
[14:15] Lina: hosted by default has short-term logs for debugging and can be configured to not retain content. we provide KMS integration for encrypting at rest with your keys, SSO/SAML, SCIM, and SOC2 reports. Private deployments give you full control over retention and network egress.
[15:00] Maya: if we use hosted and want no retention, is there a way to still get helpful trace IDs?
[15:06] Samir: yes — you can collect audit metadata without storing actual prompt text. trace ids and anonymized metrics are retained for troubleshooting.
[15:35] Lina: back to retry policy: concrete config we recommend: retries: 3, base_delay_ms: 200, max_delay_ms: 8000, jitter: full, respect_retry_after: true, idempotency_header: x-request-id. for streaming: dedupe on server or prefer short retries with client dedupe.
[16:15] Arjun: what about HTTP vs WebSocket streaming — any differences in retry semantics?
[16:20] Lina: WebSocket allows persistent connection with lower overhead but reconnection handling is similar; both require client-side handling for reconnects. WebSocket reconnection often easier to resume UI but still you'll want request ids.
[16:50] Luke: performance — can you quantify expected p95 for a small model vs a bigger 70B for a 64-token response?
[17:00] Lina: ballpark: small open models p95 80-120ms per token on modern GPUs; medium 7-13B p95 maybe 160-300ms per token; larger 70B p95 can be 300-700ms per token depending on hardware and batching. real numbers vary a lot — that's why we offered to run a test with your prompts.
[18:00] Samir: let's talk cost controls: Redwood Console has per-route budgets and token usage alerts; you can set hard caps to avoid surprises. also use max_tokens and stop sequences to constrain worst-case.
[18:40] Maya: quick question about streaming partial failures — if a payment or billing error occurs mid-stream, what happens?
[18:47] Samir: then server will return an error; treat it like any other 4xx/5xx. ensure the client shows a friendly retry or contact support message. billing errors shouldn't cause silent truncation without an error code.
[19:10] Lina: now a quick Optimize tip: for repeated prompts, enable prefix caching; for high throughput, configure batching windows and use a quantized variant for cheaper tokens. Optimize will surface model/quantization suggestions per workload.
[19:40] Arjun: can Optimize recommend batching windows? we have bursty traffic.
[19:46] Lina: yes, Optimize looks at sequence length distribution and recommends batching windows that balance latency and throughput. it'll also suggest autoscale thresholds for Dedicated.
[20:15] Maya: are there any gotchas for stop sequences and streaming?
[20:20] Lina: with streaming, stop sequences may arrive in the middle of a chunk boundary so you should implement final-chunk scanning and don't render past stop tokens. some transcriptions may omit control chars; ensure server-side enforcement of stop sequences when you require strict termination.
[21:00] [21:00] Samir: ok let's do rapid-fire Q&A.
[21:05] Luke: what's the typical plan for PII redaction?
[21:08] Tess: we use a local PII scrubber before storing logs; is that recommended?
[21:12] Lina: yes — scrub before retention. Redwood can do redaction hooks in Private; for hosted you can call redaction APIs or scrub before persistence.
[21:45] Maya: can you bump up retries for server-to-server background jobs?
[21:48] Samir: absolutely. for background jobs we recommend higher retry counts, exponential backoff with a longer max_delay, and webhook-style completion callbacks to your system.
[22:30] Arjun: what about SDK support — do SDKs include built-in retry helpers?
[22:34] Lina: our official SDKs include helpers for idempotency headers and recommend patterns; community clients may vary. we'll share sample code.
[23:00] Maya: any final notes on production hardening?
[23:05] Samir: instrument trace ids end-to-end, implement server-side idempotency, set client rate limits and backpressure, use Console budgets & alerts, and run a small pilot to collect representational latency metrics.
